heading: Toy networks superpose sparse features as near-orthogonal directions, with sparsity transitions and regular geometry
definition: in small networks with more sparse features than dimensions, features are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, with a sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry.
summary: Independent groups reproduce each part of this picture in toy models, each in its own setting: models pack more features into each dimension as sparsity rises, directions are nearly orthogonal in some settings but not under strong bottleneck pressure, and the geometry is regular (polygons, or close to an equiangular tight frame, where all pairs of directions overlap equally). None of these studies checks every part, results depend on weight decay, activation function, dropout and feature correlations, and some toy mixture-of-experts models show no clear phase change.

suggested_status.by_scale: R2 in toy models (conditional on setting). No level at <1B, 1-10B, 10-100B or >100B: counts versions.V1.studies_by_size has only 'not stated' (50); versions.V1.studies_by_family has 'other or not stated' (50) and BLOOM (1), and the BLOOM study appears only under versions.V1.coverage_by_operation.other with state cannot_determine.
suggested_status.reason: Different groups reproduce separate components of V1 in toy models, each in its own setting. Sparsity dependence: arXiv:2508.17456#R1 (toy ReLU autoencoder, n=100, m=20, density swept 1.0 to 0.1) finds features per dimension rising with sparsity, with an antipodal plateau. Regular geometry, not a sparsity transition: arXiv:2310.06301#r1 derives a regular 5-gon critical point, and arXiv:2310.06301#r4 finds a 5-gon to 6-gon posterior transition driven by sample size (600≤n≤700). Both hold at fixed high sparsity with r=2, c=6; this study does not vary sparsity. Reviewed (NeurIPS) arXiv:2505.10465#R8 reports ETF-like strongly represented vectors, with mean squared overlap about 1/m, under negative weight decay and relatively even feature frequencies. Near-orthogonality depends on bottleneck pressure. At seed 42, arXiv:2606.12629#R15 reports mean |cos| 0.052 at n=100, d=20, s=0.05, while arXiv:2606.12629#R03 reports 0.333 at n=20, d=5, s=0.05. Each of these four studies' untested-parts lines leaves out at least one component. arXiv:2508.17456 does not quantify near-orthogonality or polytope geometry. arXiv:2310.06301, arXiv:2505.10465 and arXiv:2606.12629 map no sparsity-dependent transition. Counts, from counts.json as built before the checks (studies whose labels the checks changed are still counted under their old labels): versions.V1.verdicts.supports.studies = 43; versions.V1.studies_with_limits_scope = 35 (architecture, loss, data and optimization conditions); versions.V1.studies_with_challenges = 0; versions.V1.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 2. versions.V1.studies_by_size does not resolve parameter scale. After the checks, studies_with_challenges = 0 no longer holds. The checks relabel arXiv:2510.23671#r11 and arXiv:2510.23671#r14 (no clear phase change with three experts in toy MoE setups B and C) and lw:xP7B8okCmXkmziZYb#r10 and lw:xP7B8okCmXkmziZYb#r11 (a trained two-LeakyReLU-neuron name-pair net that stores names as collinear scalar scores) as challenges. Neither study shares authors with an original. Neither is a failed replication in the original reconstruction setting. In arXiv:2510.23671, the dense single-expert models show superposition and a clear phase change over sparsity and importance (supports verdict; arXiv:2510.23671#r1, arXiv:2510.23671#r3, arXiv:2510.23671#r7, arXiv:2510.23671#r9, arXiv:2510.23671#r12). The header of lw:xP7B8okCmXkmziZYb says it is not a reproduction of the original toy-model setup. The checks also moved some V1 limits_scope verdicts to supports (lw:wMn9wSxzSs3uHiAmu sigmoid family, lw:a5wwqza2cY3W7L9cj, lw:buxBdp8NtHGgBwabv) or to none (lw:WwxG8RRHrorJgpoAk Case 4, lw:gC5J7LaEgjnohYAgh at S=0.426). The supports and limits_scope counts above are therefore pre-check figures too.
suggested_status.open_questions: A failed replication in the original reconstruction setting, or a credible measurement-artifact argument, would move the level to C. After the checks, the against section holds challenges items for arXiv:2510.23671 (arXiv:2510.23671#r11, arXiv:2510.23671#r14; three-expert toy MoE settings) and lw:xP7B8okCmXkmziZYb (lw:xP7B8okCmXkmziZYb#r10, lw:xP7B8okCmXkmziZYb#r11; two-neuron name-pair classification net). Both concern architectures or tasks other than the original reconstruction model. An independent sparsity sweep that measures near-orthogonality and polygon geometry together would show whether the full conjunction reproduces in one setting. Joint sparsity and geometry phase diagrams across decoder depth, feature dependence and training objectives would clarify the scope. Results in pretrained models with known features would let levels be assigned above toy scale.

source.title: Toy Models of Superposition
source.authors: Nelson Elhage; Tristan Hume; Catherine Olsson; Nicholas Schiefer; T. Henighan; S. Kravec; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; R. Lasenby; Dawn Drain; Carol Chen; R. Grosse; Sam McCandlish; J. Kaplan; D. Amodei; M. Wattenberg; Chris Olah

original_result.setup: They trained small linear and ReLU toy models on sparse synthetic features with fewer hidden dimensions than features, sweeping sparsity and feature importance.
original_result.result: With dense features the models keep only the most important features, like PCA; as sparsity rises, ReLU models store more features than dimensions, first as antipodal pairs (two features at opposite ends of one direction), in a phase change that also depends on relative feature importance. With equal importance, features form regular shapes (triangles, tetrahedra, pentagons using 2/5 of a dimension per feature, square antiprisms), and the antipodal-pair arrangement, at 1/2 dimension per feature, stays put over a range of sparsity (a sticky plateau).
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Superposition appeared only above a sparsity threshold, with features overlapping within mutually orthogonal, polytope-like blocks.
Regular-polygon feature layouts were proven critical points of the loss and held most Bayesian posterior mass.
Compressing a transformer compiled from a program stored its sparse embeddings non-orthogonally in shared dimensions.
With many features, trained autoencoders weighted each feature's self-reconstruction equally, with small, Gaussian-like cross-feature interference.
Feature interference grew as toy ReLU bottlenecks narrowed below the width that keeps features separate.
Class vectors were non-orthogonal when classes outnumbered bottleneck dimensions, and orthogonal when counts matched.
Features per dimension rose with sparsity, with a plateau where features sat in opposite-direction pairs.
Mutually exclusive features within a group overlapped nearly orthogonally, and cross-group superposition grew with group sparsity.
With small or negative weight decay, most features overlapped, evenly spread like an equiangular tight frame.
Standard toy models without mixture-of-experts replicated superposition and a clear phase change as sparsity varied.
Tied-weight autoencoders represented nearly all 64 features in 32 dimensions.
Losses raising error to powers above 2 gave features overlapping sparse neuron sets, spreading error evenly.
Narrow toy attention heads showed cross-variable interactions, read by the authors as compression into fewer dimensions.
In the very sparse regime, optimal autoencoders superpose, using nearly orthogonal constructions.
Features became fully represented past a sparsity-dependent width, with overlaps as small as possible (Welch bound).
At intermediate bottleneck widths, features formed opposite-direction pairs, as in the original toy model.
Distilled students' loss floors fell with sparsity, far below what one feature per dimension would allow.
Proofs show exponentially many sparse features fit in near-orthogonal directions.
In a toy autoencoder without an attention head, 20 features formed 10 evenly spread opposite-direction pairs.
Features used up every available dimension, and theory ties this to evenly spread (tight-frame) directions.
Replicating the original toy model gave more features than dimensions, nearly orthogonal with 20 hidden dimensions.
Standard training at high sparsity kept all 100 features in 20 dimensions.
A replication of the original toy model found the same sparsity-dependent superposition.
In the MemoryDT transformer, anti-correlated items pointed opposite ways; targets formed near-opposite pairs, roughly evenly spread.
Without dropout, superposition grew with sparsity, ending in a regular pentagon.
Under non-uniform sparsity, 3–4 of 5 features were superposed in 2 dimensions.
Anticorrelated features were stored in superposition as opposite-direction pairs.
Both standard ReLU and ternary-weight BitNet toy models reproduced superposition with regular geometry.
About 16–18 of 20 features fit in 10 dimensions, with interference.
ReLU-family and soft-elbow activations showed prominent superposition, described qualitatively.
ReLU-like asymmetric activations developed superposition as strongly as ReLU or more.
Losses raising error to powers above 2 gave features overlapping 5–7-neuron sets, spreading error evenly.
With 6 features in 2 dimensions, optimal hexagons gave way to smaller polygons as density rose.
With tied-ReLU or single-layer bilinear decoders, 19 of 20 runs learned symmetric, mutually orthogonal opposite-direction pairs.
With spare bottleneck capacity, paired co-activating features stayed near-orthogonal at every coupling level.
A residual ReLU network stored tokens as overlapping sparse hashes in fewer dimensions.
Cross-entropy and BCE losses produced superposition in small toy models.
With large datasets, five features formed a pentagon, a result replicated independently.
An underrepresented feature's entanglement (overlap with others) fell toward theirs as its data share rose.
In a bottleneck encoder trained with replay of past data, sparser features overlapped systematically more.
Under capacity pressure, the opposite-direction pairing rate rose from 0.068 to 0.562 as anti-correlation grew.
Polysemanticity (features sharing neurons) was absent in dense regimes, rising with sparsity into mutually orthogonal blocks.
With low dropout, superposition persisted, sometimes with fewer dimensions per feature.
A model computing a quadratic function formed one loosely ordered superposed block instead of regular polytopes.
No regular c-gon critical point was found for c>8 not divisible by 4.
Small models fluctuated, and large ones were regular only in aggregate statistics.
Superposition followed co-occurrence: it stayed within groups of never-co-occurring features, with groups in orthogonal subspaces.
Large weight decay suppressed superposition, and skewed frequencies made overlaps irregular.
Mixture-of-experts models reduced superposition and smoothed or removed the phase change.
MLPs computing AND clauses accumulated error once clauses equalled neurons.
Under L2 loss the network gave some features their own neuron and used no superposition.
When features' firing probabilities differed strongly, bands of feature norms merged, leaving no clean represented/unrepresented transition.
Correlated features formed circles and semantic clusters instead of near-orthogonal arrangements.
Constructions with separate encoder and decoder weights recovered features linearly, with highly correlated directions across features.
At high sparsity, spectral mass grew more diffuse and a few features spread across eigenspaces.
Under high bottleneck pressure, with 5 hidden dimensions, superposed features were substantially non-orthogonal.
Adversarial training dropped 70 of 100 features, reducing superposition.
Replicating the original toy model, the author found results looked significantly different with nonzero bias initialization.
In the MemoryDT transformer, instruction embeddings formed opposite-direction pairs but clustered unevenly, unlike in toy models.
Dropout reduced superposition, limited the geometry to opposite-direction pairs, and smoothed the phase transition.
Under non-uniform sparsity, at most 4 of 5 features were represented.
Superposition appeared even though features were not sparse by frequency: each occurred every other input.
Weight quantization shifted the onset and amount of superposition in BitNets.
Superposed features can be read out without being near-orthogonal; how many fit depends on the loss.
Without ReLU, target-feature-only loss recovered over 50 features in 2 dimensions, packed denser than near-orthogonality allows.
Bounded and several other activations showed little superposition, mostly opposite-direction pairs.
Symmetric, bounded or near-linear activations gave much weaker superposition than ReLU.
In a high-dimensional tanh^3 (cubed tanh) model, superposed encoder sign patterns looked independently random, not regular.
Despite more sparse features than neurons, standard L² loss just gave some features their own neuron.
Random initialization rarely found the optimal hexagon, yielding varied, irregular geometries.
Bilinear decoders with multiple layers kept superposition, but no run learned symmetric geometry.
Trained nets mostly used subtractive cancellation rather than near-orthogonal superposed directions.
Without spare bottleneck capacity, correlated features tilted toward each other or collapsed onto shared axes.
Predicting a top-k output set, the network learned random binary hashes, read like a Bloom filter.
Plain MSE gave no consistent superposition, and BCE dropped features at larger sizes.
With small finite datasets, data points rather than features were superposed.
With anti-correlation imposed, opposite-direction pairing did not simply increase with sparsity.
Moderate-to-high dropout generally reduced the superposition learned.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: The complete V1 conjunction—known sparse features exceeding dimensions, near-orthogonal storage, a sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry—in pretrained language models across parameter-size buckets.
untested.basis: versions.V1.studies_by_size contains only 'not stated'. versions.V1.studies_by_family is predominantly 'other or not stated'; the BLOOM-tagged coverage is confined to coverage_by_operation.other with state cannot_determine. The original's untested-parts line explicitly leaves generalization beyond toy models open. Transformer examples in the pack establish selected components rather than this conjunction.

untested.what: Joint sparsity-by-importance phase diagrams and geometry measurements for deep bilinear decoders, toy attention heads and compressed computation networks.
untested.basis: The untested-parts lines for these studies state fixed sparsity, no sparsity transition, or absent importance variation. versions.V1.coverage_by_operation records training, measurement and scaling but supplies no joint coverage resolving these omissions. Existing shallow reconstruction phase diagrams do not test these architectures.

untested.what: Whether gradient training realizes the specific high-capacity or non-near-orthogonal theoretical constructions under their stated assumptions. For the tied-weight odd-power autoencoder, the construction and its capacity advantage hold only for a fixed odd power m>1 in the very sparse regime p≤d^-m. At m=1 superposition gives no advantage. Whether a geometric phase transition occurs there is also not established.
untested.basis: The untested-parts lines of the representation/accessibility, odd-power-autoencoder and bundled-vector studies explicitly distinguish constructions from trained solutions. The check of arXiv:2606.18538's supports label narrows its condition to fixed odd m>1 and says training realization and a geometric phase transition remain unestablished. versions.V1.coverage_by_operation.measurement aggregates theoretical and empirical rows and does not establish training realization. The relevant construction rows are arXiv:2602.11246#r3, arXiv:2606.18538#r5 and lw:2roZtSr5TGmLjXMnT#R7.

wording_issues.issue: Under some training conditions, what is superposed is not generalizing features, or superposition is suppressed. In finite-data ReLU-output toy models with small datasets, datapoints rather than generalizing features are superposed. Large positive weight decay suppresses superposition, leaving a represented fraction of order m/n.

Near-orthogonality depends on compression, feature dependence and encoder/decoder constraints. In a replicated toy autoencoder at d=5 (seed 42; arXiv:2606.12629), mean absolute cosine between represented feature columns is 0.333–0.345. In a toy classifier with k=7 co-activating features (lw:rwu73dCE3uWjieijK), partner features align only partly at width m=2: partner cosine reaches about 0.5 (figure-derived), below a non-partner |cos| of about 0.6, though the prose says it crosses above that baseline. At m=3 and m=4 the text calls partners near-orthogonal or in avoidance. Untied, unconstrained theoretical constructions need not have near-orthogonal representations (arXiv:2602.11246).

The type of transition needs specifying. Width-driven partial-to-full representation, and sample-size-driven posterior changes at fixed high sparsity, are different from a sparsity-driven onset. Dropout makes the transition more gradual. In toy MoEs, phase changes become continuous or mixed, and are absent in the three-expert settings of architectures B and C (r11, r14). The checks label those absent-transition settings challenges, not limits_scope. Strong firing-probability inequality merges representation bands.

This can mean low-dimensional polygons, tight frames, block structure, or only regular aggregate statistics. Deeper bilinear decoders produce asymmetric arrangements, and the quadratic model has a less-ordered block. In large permutation-symmetric models, individual off-diagonal weights can resemble noise despite regular aggregate statistics. The authors' differently structured, forward-engineered construction closely matches trained reconstruction loss; this is a method comparison, not itself a V1 result. High-sparsity spectral localization is approximate.

Marginal occurrence frequency does not fully specify the relevant data structure. In grouped-feature autoencoders, mutual exclusivity and co-occurrence change which features overlap. For a designated anti-correlated pair at d=2–8, antipodal incidence (a fraction of converged runs) is 1.00 at S=0.5 for anti-correlation ≥0.25 and mostly falls as sparsity rises, though not monotonically. These values are figure-derived; at S=0.99, strict exclusivity gives d=2 0.14 and d=8 0.17. The authors call anti-correlation the primary driver and say the relationship is not uniform across sparsity and dimension. A composed-feature 4→2 model learns antipodal pairs when each feature occurs every other draw (S≈0.5); the checks read this as support for V1. That author also qualifies reading sparsity as occurrence frequency.

wording_issues.phrase: in small networks with more sparse features than dimensions
wording_issues.issue: This condition alone does not ensure the reported storage mechanism. Loss, readout, activation and computational task matter. L2 compressed computation can learn the naive solution. In single-hidden-layer MLPs computing 4-variable AND clauses, error accumulates as clause count approaches neuron count, and the authors state that these networks do not really achieve superposition. Training error alone does not measure V1's storage geometry.

method_sensitivity.what: Changing L2 to higher loss exponents changes compressed computation from selective feature handling to distributed error and overlapping codewords. Linear-readout MSE, BCE and CE select different embeddings; target-only loss supports storage under different interference requirements.

Replacing ReLU changes how much superposition forms, when it forms, and which features it reaches. ReLU-like asymmetric functions keep or strengthen it. Several bounded, symmetric or hard functions give limited or small-amplitude superposition. The earlier survey reports strong superposition for sigmoid, hard sigmoid, softsign and logsigmoid, concentrated in unimportant features; its author flags this as a possible bug. The later survey reports little superposition for bounded outputs. Both surveys are qualitative, and some functions failed to converge.

method_sensitivity.factor: Bottleneck width, decoder depth and expert routing
method_sensitivity.what: Bottleneck pressure changes measured cosine overlap. Increasing bilinear decoder depth replaces symmetric arrangements with asymmetric ones. Expert routing reduces superposition and confines it within experts, and features per dimension fall as expert count rises. MoE phase changes become more continuous: setup B with two experts has a mixed region at S≈0.5–0.7, and setup C has one at S≈0.48–0.7. With three experts in setups B and C, the paper reports no clear phase change.

Large positive weight decay suppresses represented-feature coverage; small or negative decay supports extensive overlap. Adversarial training reduces represented-feature counts relative to standard training at matched sparsity.

Dropout changes overlap, basis alignment and transition shape. In the 5→2 and 20→5 toy autoencoders: dropout reduces superposition; at p=0.4 features align with the basis; the 20→5 transition with varying importance becomes gradual. Dense inputs with varying importance can instead show more superposition. Lowering dropout from p=0.4 to p=0.15 gives intermediate superposition and performance; no increase above the no-dropout model is reported. In a separate ReLU output model, more dropout generally gives higher dimensions per feature. Low dropout can give lower dimensions per feature than no dropout at certain sparsities. Sparse features become axis-aligned above about 50% dropout, and the privileged-basis effect is weaker or absent for dense features.

Group dependence decides whether features overlap within groups, separate into subspaces or form circles. For correlated partners with k=7 features, width changes the outcome (all values figure-derived). At m=2, partner cosine reaches about 0.5, below a non-partner |cos| of about 0.6; the prose says it crosses above. At m=3 and m=4, partners are about −0.23 and −0.53 at coupling t=1, which the authors call near-orthogonal or avoidance. The designated-pair antipodal fraction rises from 0.068 at anti-correlation 0 to 0.562 under strict exclusivity, aggregated over sparsity and dimension. The authors call anti-correlation the primary driver, with sparsity and bottleneck dimension modulating it. At d=2–8, incidence is 1.00 at S=0.5 for anti-correlation ≥0.25 and mostly falls as sparsity rises, not monotonically (figure-derived).

Increasing firing-probability inequality changes critical width and can erase norm-band separation. Skewed frequencies increase overlap heterogeneity. Non-uniform sparsity changes which features are represented: constant-importance Case 4 omits the least-sparse features. The represented features remain mostly superposed, with a few seed-dependent exceptions.
Bias initialization changes replication outcomes. Random versus favorable polygon initialization changes which geometries training reaches and whether dimensions or neurons collapse.
Dataset size changes whether models store examples or generalizing features. Repeated examples occupy embedding capacity and displace generalizing features.

method_sensitivity.factor: Geometry assumptions and scale of regularity
method_sensitivity.what: Norm constraints change whether theoretical recovery requires near-orthogonal directions. Increasing feature count improves concentration of aggregate interference statistics, while high sparsity can weaken exact spectral localization.

status_amendment.public_note: After the checks, parts of two studies now count as challenges to this version: some three-expert mixture-of-experts toy models show no clear phase change, and a tiny two-neuron network stores names as collinear scores rather than near-orthogonal directions. Both use architectures or tasks that differ from the original setup and neither is a failed replication of it, so the level stays R2.
